transcript.text:
2/3=4/6

Multiply both the numerator and denominator by 2: 2 × 2 = 4, and 3 × 2 = 6.
I still don't get why you multiply both numbers by the same thing.

You multiply both by the same number because you’re not changing the amount—you’re just cutting the whole into more, smaller pieces.

Think of a pizza:

2/3 means 2 out of 3 equal slices.

If you cut every slice into 2 smaller pieces, you now have 6 total pieces.

Your original 2 slices become 4 smaller pieces.

So:

2/3 = 4/6

The denominator changed from 3 to 6 because the pizza was cut twice as finely. To keep the same fraction of the pizza, the numerator must also double: from 2 pieces to 4 pieces.

Mathematically, multiplying top and bottom by 2 is the same as multiplying by 2/2, which equals 1:

2/3 × 2/2 = 4/6

Since 2/2 = 1, the value stays the same. That is why equivalent fractions require the same multiplier for numerator and denominator.
I still don't get why multiplying the top and bottom by the same number works if the numbers are getting bigger.

Yes—the numbers get bigger, but the pieces get smaller at exactly the same rate. The fraction describes a proportion, not just a count of pieces.

For 2/3:

The bottom number, 3, says: “cut the whole into 3 equal parts.”

The top number, 2, says: “take 2 of those parts.”

If you multiply both by 2, you are cutting every one of the 3 parts into 2 smaller pieces:

text
2/3:
[██][██][ ]
 2 shaded out of 3 parts

4/6:
[█|█][█|█][ | ]
 4 shaded out of 6 smaller parts

You now have twice as many pieces total (6 instead of 3), so to keep the same amount shaded, you must also have twice as many shaded pieces (4 instead of 2). The shaded area is unchanged.

Another way to see it:

2/3 × 2/2 = 4/6

You are multiplying by 2/2, which equals 1. Multiplying something by 1 does not change its value—it only changes how it is written.

So 2/3 and 4/6 are different labels for the same amount: two-thirds.
